slides.headline: “If I bring a toy into the bedroom, will my partner *feel replaced?*”
slides.lead: The question people are too shy to ask. Swipe.

slides.headline: Underneath it is one question: *“Am I not enough?”*
slides.body: It’s the most common reaction. Naming it out loud takes most of the sting out before the conversation even starts.
slides.note: From intimova.ng: How to talk to your partner about sex toys.

slides.headline: A toy adds to what you share. *It doesn’t replace anyone.*
slides.body: It adds sensation, playfulness and curiosity to something you already have. It isn’t competition: it’s a shared idea you explore on the same team.

slides.kicker: WHY IT CAN BRING YOU CLOSER
slides.headline: Couples who use toys together often report *feeling closer.*
slides.body: Because the conversation itself builds trust.

slides.headline: Lead with “us”. *Pick a calm, clothed moment.*
slides.body: “I love what we have. I’d love to add a little play to it.” An invitation, not a verdict. Then listen more than you pitch.

slides.headline: You’re not replacing them. *You’re inviting them in.*

“If I bring a toy into the bedroom, will my partner feel replaced?”

The question people are too shy to ask. Underneath it is usually one worry: “am I not enough?” Name it out loud.

A toy adds sensation and play to what you already share; it doesn’t replace anyone. Couples who use toys together often report feeling closer, because the conversation itself builds trust.

How to say it: a calm, clothed moment, and lead with “us”. “I love what we have. I’d love to add a little play to it.”
